newsitem.title: INDIA: Trends show Sikh party ahead in India Punjab polls.
newsitem.headline: Trends show Sikh party ahead in India Punjab polls.

text.p: The pro-Sikh Akali Dal party of former chief minister Prakash Singh Badal took a crucial early lead in key local polls in India's northern state of Punjab, officials said on Sunday.
The state's chief electoral officer Brajendra Singh said the right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), an ally of the Akali Dal, won the first seat declared at 4.00 p.m (1030 GMT).
Trends from counting in 49 other constituencies of the 117-member state assembly showed the Akali Dal was leading in 34, he added.
The BJP, which won a seat from the city of Jallandhar, was leading in six other constituencies while the ruling Congress party was ahead in three, officials said.
Election officials began counting votes early on Sunday amid tight security across the state. Results were expected to be announced by late evening.
More than 65 percent of Punjab's 15 million voters turned out on Friday in a remarkably peaceful election for the state assembly that is expected to thrust the Akali Dal party into power.
"The (combination) will get 100 seats of which 15 will belong to the BJP," said Kanwaljit Singh, a Akali Dal candidate from Banur constituency and a former state minister.
The BJP is contesting 25 seats while Akali Dal has put up candidates in the remaining 92 constituencies.

The polls for the state assembly were the first in two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatist violence. Officials said, however, that the state's political groups were too badly divided to ensure badly-needed stability.
But Sukbhir Grewal, an independent political analyst, said: "There is no reason to believe that the Akali Dal will do anything to retard the peace process in Punjab."
The Akali Dal's poll alliance with BJP was seen as offering a chance to Punjab's two main communities -- Hindus and Sikhs -- to heal their mistrust, analysts said.
"The Akali Dal holds the best bet for forging Hindu-Sikh unity in Punjab," Kanwaljit Singh said. "The Akali Dal has changed its focus from pro-Sikh to pro-Punjab party."
"These elections will prove (to be a) triumph for Punjabi unity," said Balramji Das Tandon, a BJP candidate in the Rajpura constitency.
But Raj Khurana, a Congress Party candidate and Tandon's rival in Rajpura, was confident that his party would form the next government.
Punjab's ruling Congress party, led by the state's first woman chief minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal, claims credit for the virtual weeding out of Sikh militancy from the region.
Sikh separatist violence peaked after Indian troops were sent into the Golden Temple in Amritsar in 1984 to flush out militants holed up in the Sikhs' holiest shrine.
Then-prime minister Indira Gandhi was killed by two Sikh bodyguards on October 31, 1984, in what was believed to be a revenge killing for the army assault.
The state polls in 1992, which revived local democracy after more than a decade of separatist violence, took place in an atmosphere of fear and overwhelming security.
